---
title: "Circuit Models, Subsystems, and Reuse"
---

::: {.callout-warning}
## CONVERGING target concept

This page explains the `CONVERGING` target for structured circuit authoring.
The authoring API, its structural identity integration, and certified diagrams
have an integrated implementation baseline but are not Human-accepted. The
[central evidence status](../contracts/index.qmd#implementation-evidence-status)
distinguishes scoped checks from whole-course execution.

Accepted numerical operations, physical component models, units, evidence
workspace, and existing Result meanings are not reopened. Exact assembly
belongs to the [CircuitPlan Assembly Contract](../contracts/circuit-plan-assembly.qmd);
diagram behavior belongs to the
[diagram contract](../contracts/automatic-semantic-circuit-diagram-layout.qmd);
exact input and batch behavior belongs to the
[Parameter System contract](../contracts/parameter-system.qmd).
:::

## Begin with the physical circuit

Suppose the circuit is a grounded parallel LC resonator connected through a
coupling capacitor to a terminated Port. Before choosing a solver, an author
must be able to answer:

- Which capacitor, inductor, coupler, ground, and Port exist?
- Which terminals share one electrical node?
- Which parts form the resonator subsystem?
- Which resonator boundary may the parent circuit connect to?

Those are authored circuit facts. A resonance frequency, a transformed
coordinate, or a plotted response is an analysis result or analysis choice;
none can supply the missing model structure after the fact.

The intended review outcome has two related but noninterchangeable parts. The
diagram must be generated from that authored Plan and checked for visible
electrical and ownership correspondence, while complete invisible declarations
remain verified source evidence. Any analytical Result must separately name
the View and request selected from the same Plan. A hand-maintained picture
cannot replace the generated projection, and the generated projection cannot
stand in for an analysis Result.

## One Plan supplies two projections {#plan-as-physical-authority}

`CircuitPlan` is the sole root authority. It records the complete electrical
network and the structure the author deliberately assigned to it. The same
authored Plan is the source for two independent uses:

1. The Automatic Semantic Circuit Diagram Layout System (ASCDLS) captures an
   immutable snapshot without sealing or mutating the authoring object, then
   derives an authoring or compiled diagram and checks its correspondence.
2. `CircuitRun` separately seals the Plan for analysis and supplies
   `run.original`; an analysis may keep that original network or derive a
   `NetworkViewRef`, then submit a Solve, Evaluate, or Optimization request.

A diagram is never the solver input, and a selected analysis View is never a
new physical circuit. Rendering does not create, choose, or mutate a View.

Three assembly scopes use the same electrical vocabulary:

| Scope | Circuit question it answers |
|---|---|
| root `CircuitPlan` | What is the complete circuit, including logical Ports? |
| inline `SubsystemPlan` | Which parts belong together in this one Plan? |
| Library `CompositePlan` | Which owned structure should be reusable as one component? |

SCNSim never infers a Subsystem from names, values, visual proximity, graph
shape, or modes. A Composite is not an opaque electrical box: its public
boundary controls access, while native children remain present in compilation
and diagram evidence.

## Why a shared node needs a bus—and only sometimes a tap

In a parallel LC resonator, the capacitor and inductor share a signal node and
ground. A `bus()` names or holds that shared electrical net, and ordinary
wiring connects directly to that bus. A `tap()` is needed only when one contact
on the same bus must be named independently, such as three feedline contacts
whose visual order the author wants to review. It never creates a separate
node.

A `PinRef` is different again: it is a native component terminal or a
parent-facing boundary exposed by a child scope. The child may expose a pin
with the ID `tap`, but the returned object is still a `PinRef`, not a `TapRef`.
A `CoordinateRef` belongs to analysis and cannot be used as a wire endpoint.

A Python variable such as `resonator_bus` is only the Notebook's local handle;
the authored `id="terminal"` is the identity scoped inside its owner. When the
parent later links its `resonator_root_bus` to the child's exposed `terminal`,
the two handles resolve to one electrical node. A single link may join three or
more eligible endpoints when they all belong to that same zero-wire
connection. The child pin preserves the owned boundary, while the root bus
preserves parent-owned assembly and gives later analysis a public root
coordinate; the link creates no extra element or electrical node.

The target grammar makes each role explicit:

- `add()` registers a physical part; it does not connect that part;
- `series()`, `parallel()`, and `branch()` place real component bodies while
  recording electrical incidence and readable authored structure;
- `bus()` expresses one net, while `tap()` optionally names one contact on it;
- `link()` makes one zero-component conductive connection among two or more
  eligible endpoints;
- `ground_pins()` deliberately grounds one or more eligible pins;
- `couple_inductive()` records an oriented nonconductive relation; and
- `subsystem()` creates an explicitly owned inline scope.

These structures are not labels applied after arbitrary wiring. `series()`
orders one chain; `parallel()` gives several chains the same endpoint pair;
`branch()` adds the explicit side-branch role even when its incidence could be
written as a series from that bus. None declares current direction. A `link()`
is different: it contains no component and only joins existing endpoints.

`scope.ground` is the circuit's canonical electrical reference expressed as a
local endpoint. It is not a catalog component or a page-wide drawing rail.

## Three grounding responsibilities

Grounding is explicit, but it is not one universal wiring recipe:

1. An **intrinsically grounded subsystem** connects a real local branch to
   `scope.ground`. Its ground belongs to the subsystem definition, so the
   parent does not ground that terminal again.
2. An **externally grounded module** exposes an ordinary return bus as a public
   `PinRef`. The parent applies `ground_pins(pins=(return_pin,))`; this grounds
   the pin's whole connected net without pretending the child was intrinsically
   grounded. A bus called `ground` is still ordinary until that declaration.
3. A **logical Port** supplies its own declared load/reference to ground. The
   Port has no public ground pin and needs no extra grounding wire.

All three resolve to the same canonical reference for compilation. The diagram
still shows the local branch, parent-side ground attachment, or Port load where
it was authored. A multi-pin `ground_pins()` call may ground several legitimate
return nets, but its tuple order and batching do not create another ground
domain or a shared drawing rail.

The diagram derives separate ground occurrences from structural terminations,
not one ground tree per scope. A Parallel's shared grounded end rail has one
glyph; separate shunts, including those at both terminals of a floating
network, keep local glyphs of their own. `composition.ground_side(...)` chooses
the displayed side of an eligible grounded structure or parent-applied ground
pin. It may rotate a structure but never reverses its electrical reference or
creates another ground domain. Port loads keep their own graphical role.

`link()` and `ground_pins()` respect ownership. A parent may use its own bus or
tap and an immediate child's public pin; it may not reach through that pin to a
private child bus. Electrical aliases do not erase those owner-local handles.
They also do not permit a later link to short two distinct buses in the
invoking scope, a physical component, or a Port to ground. The target validates
the complete affected Plan before committing the declaration, so a rejected
operation leaves the editable model unchanged and its proposed ID reusable.

## Why a child exposes a public pin

A parent must not reach into a child and wire a private capacitor terminal or
private bus.
Instead, `expose_pin()` publishes one parent-facing boundary at an internal
node. The pin and that internal bus are the same electrical boundary; exposure
does not add a component or a second wire.

Other public boundaries are deliberately different:

- `expose_coordinate()` publishes an eligible analysis coordinate;
- `expose_inductive_branch()` publishes an oriented branch for mutual
  coupling; and
- a Library Composite may publish an independently defined, physically bound
  parameter that a later operation may vary.

Private buses, taps, and leaves remain private. One internal node may expose
several differently named ordinary public pins. For example, `plus_1` and
`plus_2` can denote the same internal bus while providing distinct public
boundaries. No component, Coordinate, or degree of freedom is added, and the
names do not assign physical input/output roles. Their external wiring groups
remain owner-local: a left coupling and a right probe can share voltage through
the child's real internal wire without becoming one parent wiring group.

Selecting two terminals of a complete multi-terminal part with `.between()` is
needed only when the author uses that whole body once inside a structure. It is
optional when the complete body remains an independent scope peer. Selecting
intrinsically equivalent pins rejects; parent-commoned nets alone do not make
two child pins intrinsically equivalent. In either
case it does not replace an IDC or multi-conductor line with a scalar equivalent;
all public terminals and native coefficients remain explicit.

An ordinary two-terminal native body must belong to exactly one structure. A
complete Composite occurrence or native multi-terminal body may instead remain
an independent peer. Native required pins remain bound; Composite public pins
may be partially or entirely externally open without inventing a load or wire.
A grounded Composite is already structurally complete because its private native
leaves were assembled inside its ownership boundary. The three built-in grounded
resonators expose `terminal_1` and `terminal_2` on that same intrinsic Bus;
either or both may remain visibly open, and their equivalent pair cannot be a
`.between()` selection. They need no second structural wrapper. Floating pins
remain distinct and custom Libraries keep their declared pin names.
A legal assembly need not be numerically solvable.

The [shared assembly contract](../contracts/circuit-plan-assembly.qmd) owns
these modeling rules. Parameter resolution, Calculation, and diagrams consume
that model independently: numerical use does not load diagram modules or
require a successful drawing. Presentation settings and rendering failures
never change the Plan or its numerical requests.

## Fixed values come before public parameters

A fixed physical value can be written directly on a native component. That is
the clearest choice when the learning task or model does not need to vary it.
The Tutorial therefore uses literal C and L values in Chapters 1–3.

An independent `ParameterRef` becomes useful when a learning task needs an
externally addressable physical value—for example, a selected point, a sweep,
or Optimization. Chapter 4 first defines the ref outside any Plan. The Plan
adopts it only when a registered component's real physical field consumes it.
Allocating a definition or mentioning the ref in a `ParameterSet` creates no
Plan binding.

A reusable Library Composite may expose an already-bound ref as a declared
public input. That boundary returns the original ref without opening private
children. One ref may deliberately feed several physical fields; equal values
held by different refs remain independent. Literals remain fixed and do not
become parameters automatically.

See [Units, Parameters, and Optimization](units-parameters-and-optimization.qmd)
for the distinction between baseline value, public parameter, operation-time
parameter set, and optimization variable.

## Reuse keeps the same structure {#composite-as-reuse-boundary}

The inline resonator is a deliberately grouped child inside one Plan, not yet
a reusable Library component. Once it is understood there, a Library author
may express the same structure inside a `CompositePlan` and publish a factory.
The consumer receives one `ComponentInstance` with only its declared public
pins, coordinates, branches, and parameters.

```text
inline SubsystemPlan
  = one Plan-owned hierarchy used here

Library CompositePlan -> ComponentInstance
  = one factory-owned hierarchy reusable elsewhere
```

Moving an inline hierarchy into a reusable Composite may preserve values and
electrical connectivity, but it changes ownership, provenance, Plan identity,
and related semantic identities. The target makes no cross-source digest
invariance promise.

## A diagram checks the declaration, not the research intent

The clean authoring diagram shows conventional native parts, wires, junctions,
local grounds, Ports, physical couplings, ownership regions, and visible
cross-boundary incidence. It does not cover the schematic with operator IDs,
link-call history, bus/tap names, or exposure metadata. Those complete authored
facts remain separately available in the audit's verified source rows. The
compiled diagram instead explains deterministic compiler expansion. Neither
projection is another circuit definition.

Automatic layout gives every parallel group a vertical electrical path by
default, with its branches left-to-right. A hint on that parallel may rotate it
to horizontal paths; changing the parent scope axis does not rotate the child
parallel implicitly. These are reading conventions only and never reverse
ordered pins or series members.

### Compose the drawing without reauthoring the circuit

`SchematicComposition` is a presentation recipe over existing Blocks and their
attachment boundaries. Blocks are the Plan's scope peers and assembly
structures, not new physical components. A structure's start/end attachment is
different from another structure's attachment on the same Bus. Public Pins,
Ports, and authored Taps select their existing contacts; the Bus itself adds no
extra arm. These attachments are not electrical nodes or analysis coordinates.

`SchematicComposition(plan=plan)`, `automatic(plan=plan, hints=None)`, and
a missing layout share one fixed Default path. Explicit per-field settings win;
omitted fields receive stable defaults. The constructor is useful for changing
just one axis or Port side: it does not require a complete manual configuration.
`show()` and inventory/wiring reads remain nonmutating.

Wiring replacement is a complete-group operation. Use
`replace_wiring(at=bus_or_link_or_public_pin)` to specify connected straight,
L, T, and Cross primitives for that group. Every actual attachment and requested
arm must be connected once; Default never guesses wires missing from an
explicit replacement. A Subsystem Pin selects parent-facing wiring; a
ComponentInstance Pin selects its occurrence-owner group, not child-private
wiring. Aliases share one authority. An ambiguous Tap requires an explicit
structure boundary rather than an arbitrary contact choice.

The existing single-pin readout can hang beneath a parent T while another T
and L connect to the floating network's coupling structures. No second public
Pin or electrical change is needed. Resolve boundary directions from explicit
settings or parent arms first; the child then supplies one complete measured
payload with upright labels, final public anchors, local grounds, and reserved
exits. The parent translates it whole without rewriting private contents.

Port presentation retains eight root-frame poses:
`port_orientation(port, boundary_side=..., load_side=...)` atomically sets the
hollow-marker side and perpendicular T-to-load/ground direction.
`port_side()` preserves an explicit compatible load side; incompatible changes
reject without partial update. `ground_side()` is not a Port control.
Without explicit settings, the selected wiring arm or intrinsic incidence
determines the marker side, then the scope's leading side if needed. Horizontal
Ports default loads downward; vertical Ports default them rightward. Outside
wiring attaches to the complete Port's circuit-facing lead end.

Default keeps horizontal Series, vertical Parallel with branches left-to-right,
and declared peer order along the scope axis. Applicable explicit tap order
precedes stable declared contact order. Two contacts use straight/L, three use
a compatible T or the fixed scope branch, four distinct directions use Cross
and other four-contact groups use connected Ts, and larger groups use a fixed
T chain. Compatible arms are assigned first, then remaining contacts and arms
in stable source/cardinal order. Default uses the same public builders as
explicit recipes; it does not enumerate or score alternatives.

Placement reserves measured Blocks, junction subtrees, Ports/loads/text,
connectors, and coupling-guide strips before drawing. Branch extents can offset
rows and enlarge later columns rather than forcing top-aligned boxes. A stable
spanning traversal places each body once while all remaining edges and cycles
retain reserved closure tracks. Channels and lanes follow stable
group/connection order; direct paths, prescribed bends, and channel/perimeter
routes are constructed arithmetically.

There is no authoring visibility-graph search, pose candidate selection,
backtracking, routing-order retry, or readability score. Different-net crossings
retain jumps; same-net routes cannot acquire incidental bridges or lose
requested junction arms or loop edges. Unsupported fixed geometry fails with
its actual scope, Block, junction, or constraint. It neither falls back to
search nor labels the physical circuit invalid. No universal placement or
numerical timing threshold is promised.

The existing five-map `SchematicLayout` convenience feeds the same fixed
Default setters. No entry point exposes coordinates, lengths, sizes, or gaps.
A changed Plan makes an old composition stale. Rendering captures one exact
Plan, effective point, and settings without mutating caller state or old results.
Authoring `diagram.composition` is the detached immutable completed recipe;
compiled diagrams expose `None`. Its inspection survives live Plan edits.
`to_composition(plan=plan)` checks exact Plan identity and returns a new fixed
editable recipe without exposing private editable contents. Reuse at another
single point remeasures/reroutes, not pixels, and may be incompatible. There is
no global reset-to-auto; create a fresh partial composition for new settings.

The exact public operations and capstone recipe remain in the
[composition contract](../contracts/automatic-semantic-circuit-diagram-layout.qmd#schematic-composition).

### Keep composition checks separate from circuit review

Authoring labels are readable projections, not rounded model inputs. Scalar
values use six significant digits with Decimal half-even rounding and supported
engineering prefixes; exact values remain in source evidence. The audit checks
the displayed text and units in that same display projection, not a numerical
tolerance. Compiled scientific coefficients retain their exact evidence path.

An N=1 CPW Box shows kind/local ID, length when values are enabled, and
the section count (`1 section` or `<N> sections`) always. Its two visible ends
do not claim ordered head/tail names;
the exact identities and RLGC stay source-verified. MTL keeps its necessary
ordered conductor/terminal evidence. Compact child frames reserve only needed
route lanes and measured labels, grounds, borders, and escapes before the
parent translates the complete child. Open public stubs are checked from real
ink and terminal incidence; a cut required wire is not an open-pin exception.

Review remains three separate questions:

1. **A — electrical correspondence:** do visible bodies, terminals, wires,
   grounds, Ports, couplings, and enabled values match the declared or compiled
   electrical evidence?
2. **B — visible ownership correspondence:** do visible regions, containment,
   leaf and Port ownership, and boundary crossings match the expected visible
   ownership evidence?
3. **C — design intent:** is this actually the circuit the Human meant to
   model?

Separate layout-constraint verification checks that requested shapes and sides
actually appear in the visible geometry: two Ts can pass electrical A yet
violate an explicit Cross request. A/B still reconstruct actual visible ink,
not hidden expected composition or ownership maps.

A/B can detect a projection mismatch. They do not pretend that invisible
authoring history was reconstructed from the image: complete operator,
exposure, bus/tap, and parameter-binding records are labelled source/provenance
evidence. Only the Human can answer C. None of the three proves that a selected
View, unrelated calculation/request override, solver, optimization, or physical
approximation is correct.

  point or an ordered parameter space without mutating the Plan.

  understood inline subsystem into a reusable Library Composite.
- [Chapter 11](../../examples/tutorials/11_review_customize_schematic.qmd)

  complete feedline/readout/floating capstone, reviews its Plan diagram, and
  only then selects a probe-compensated analysis View.
